extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American journalism history; historians of the early 19th-century press
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, practices, and evaluative criteria for American newspapers and news production in the period 1801–1833, covering news-gathering, editorial practice, format, technology, circulation, and business model. Useful for assessing how well a paper of the period met contemporary expectations for timeliness, content mix, and professional practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness as a defining quality of news
rubrics_metrics.description: A growing feeling for timeliness as a quality of news caused papers to employ express riders, private pony express, and government express posts; timeliness became a valued characteristic of news publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jackson's 1829 message carried by private pony express reached Baltimore in 1.5 hours and New York in ~20 hours; 1825 government 'express post' cut long-route times drastically. Anti-pattern: long delays due to irregular mails (some western towns went weeks without postal service). Scoring note: evaluate a paper by how actively it pursued faster delivery (use of expresses/news-boat) and by how current its reports were relative to event dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on and use of the postal system
rubrics_metrics.description: The web of postal routes was a basic necessity to rapid newspaper development; newspapers depended heavily on the mails for receiving other papers and distributing their own product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: assess whether the paper leveraged postal routes and expressed complaints/advocated improvements when mail irregularities hindered news. Example: more than ninety percent of mails consisted of newspapers by the end of the period. Anti-pattern: expecting reliable service where mail was irregular—this limited timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-news gathering techniques (news-boat / boarding ships)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt handling of foreign news via boarding incoming ships and receiving packets before the ship reached harbor (the news-boat technique) became an important method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Samuel Topliff's continuously manned boat (Boston, 1811); New York papers joined to fund a news-boat fleet; competition led to individual schooners/clippers. Scoring: whether a paper participated in or utilized these techniques and how effectively it secured foreign dispatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority shift: foreign news versus domestic news
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier dominance of foreign news in American papers gave way to increased importance of domestic news (especially during the War of 1812–14), with national politics becoming the great continuous story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate content mix: proportion of foreign dispatches versus domestic reports and political coverage. Anti-pattern: treating foreign news as the only 'real' news when domestic events (wars, elections) were of dominant public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local/home news production (or neglect thereof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Local or home news remained largely underdeveloped; smaller papers often printed only deaths, marriages, and occasional local incidents and usually did not 'manufacture' news at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: a strong local paper should produce original home reporting rather than rely entirely on received papers. Anti-pattern: editors considering local news 'funny' or unimportant and filling space with reprinted foreign items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercantile/ship news specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercantile newspapers prioritized marine and shipping news and commodity information over other local events; some mercantile papers ignored floods, earthquakes, or wars but tracked ship clearances obsessively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess by genre: mercantile papers should be judged by accuracy and timeliness of shipping and price information. Anti-pattern: poor reporting of local commodity or stock prices despite claiming mercantile focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Washington news and the value of capital correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: Washington news was widely valued; many papers relied on reprinting from capital papers but the best supplied their own correspondents or used early Washington bureaus to cover Congress and official business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reliance on National Intelligencer, United States Telegraph, Globe; early correspondents such as Matthew L. Davis ('The Spy in Washington') and Elias Kingman's bureau (from 1822). Scoring: presence/quality of Washington reporting and whether the paper used stenographic or on-the-ground reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: War correspondence: mostly informal and haphazard
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized war correspondence was largely absent; reports of battles often arrived by devious means and some proto-war-correspondents (e.g., James M. Bradford) acted as occasional on-the-scene reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: evaluate whether a paper made efforts to secure reliable eyewitness or official dispatches during conflicts. Anti-pattern: reliance solely on delayed secondhand reports failing to convey contemporaneous events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial column norms and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial columns were typically placed under the local heading, commonly short single paragraphs, and mixed with news; editorializing and 'pilfering paragraphs' from other papers were common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good editorials were comparatively rare; evaluate editorials for originality, information quality, taste, and tendency to copy content from elsewhere. Anti-patterns: poorly informed or tasteless editorials and frequent unacknowledged borrowing from other papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political partisanship as a content driver
rubrics_metrics.description: Politics dominated most newspapers—news, essays, letters, and editorial paragraphs were chiefly political, and many papers served as party organs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political alignment, transparency about partisan stance, and whether political advocacy compromised basic news functions. Note legal and reputational risks (e.g., libel suits) for strongly partisan editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size, make-up, and page allocation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical papers retained a four-page format with advertising often taking three-fourths of the first page; a common layout placed foreign/domestic news on page two, editorials/local items on page three, and advertising on the last page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the paper's make-up conforms to period norms and whether the allocation served readers' needs. Example: metropolitan dailies enlarged page area and columns as press facilities improved. Anti-pattern: ad space crowding out essential news or vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline development and display conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines showed little development; most stories used small-type heads, with occasional larger or dramatic heads for major events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: whether headline use is appropriate to event importance; avoid anachronistic expectations for sensational modern-style headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features and miscellany inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers commonly included essays, anecdotes, poetry, and a 'poet's corner' or similar features, often under fanciful departmental headings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the quality and placement of features as part of reader appeal. Anti-pattern: filler miscellany that displaces significant local or political reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising volume, rates, and typography
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical papers devoted more than half their space to advertising (often up to four-fifths); rates were low (e.g., fifty cents a square for first insertion), and advertising typography resembled modern classified pages with small type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the paper's sustainability and reader impact given advertising load; note that legal notices were particularly profitable. Anti-pattern: overly compressed display that makes ads unreadable or dominates editorial space to the detriment of news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation scale and subscription practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulations were generally small (averages around 1,000; biggest ~4,500 in 1833); subscription prices varied by frequency and region; settlement could be in produce and delinquency was common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing reach, consider regional constraints, payment-in-kind practices, and high delinquency (many papers accumulated large bad subscription debts). Scoring: circulation claims vs verifiable post-office or proprietor records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press, papermaking, ink, and type technology standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Technological improvements (Columbian press, steam-driven cylinder presses like Napier and Hoe double-cylinder, Fourdrinier paper machine, industrial ink manufacturing, and machine type-casting) materially affected production capacity and print quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a paper adopted available technologies appropriate for its market (e.g., use of steam press for higher circulation). Example: Napier press (2,000/h) in 1825; Hoe double-cylinder increased capacity. Anti-pattern: refusal to modernize leading to limited circulation or poorer print quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personnel and role expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The apprentice system dominated; editors were often printers who acted as reporters, typesetters, pressmen, circulation and advertising managers; specialized reporters were rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess staffing model for adequacy: presence of dedicated reporters, ship-news men, or congressional reporters is a positive sign. Anti-pattern: single-person operations unable to produce timely or varied reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperative news-gathering and early press associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers sometimes cooperated—jointly funding news-boats or express riders—foreshadowing later press associations and cooperative news gathering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate participation in cooperative efforts as an indicator of resourcefulness and commitment to timeliness. Anti-pattern: insular papers that refused to collaborate and thus missed key dispatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business model dependence on advertising and legal notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Because rates and subscriptions were low, advertising (including long-term yearly contracts) and legal notices provided primary revenue necessary for survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a paper's financial viability by its ad base and proportion of legal notices; anti-patterns include overreliance on unstable subscription payments and large delinquent accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial ethics and legal exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Politically outspoken editors sometimes incurred libel suits; strong editorial advocacy brought reputational and legal risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate editorial content for factual basis and libel risk; historical examples include papers accumulating libel suits. Scoring: balance of forceful opinion and defensible factual reporting.
